name: Fatima Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Fatima. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government, and what you say is confidential. What does a normal day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Ashgrove by seven. First the hen houses, walking through to check the birds, picking out any floor eggs, making sure the feeders and drinkers are working. Then most of the morning I'm in the packing room. The grader machine sorts the eggs by size, and I check for cracks and dirty ones and pack the trays for the shops.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to farm work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I cooked at the Crossroads Diner for twenty-five years, breakfasts for lorry drivers mostly. When the bypass opened, the traffic went and the diner closed within a year. Mrs Mercer from Ashgrove used to buy her breakfast from me, and she said, come and pack eggs, you're good with your hands and you're never late.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the hens more than I thought. They each have their ways. What's hard is how much I still don't know about them. When a hen looks poorly, Dev, the stockman, knows what it is straight away, and I'm still asking. And the dust in the sheds gets in my chest in winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a lot of worry over nothing. I'd say it to the ladies in the packing room, and at our community centre on Sunday. My daughter would probably post something, I'd leave that to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be pleased. It means my job carries on until I stop at sixty-six, and Raj keeps driving his taxi. I use the AI sometimes, my daughter Sana showed me, to check what's wrong with a hen or to scale up a recipe for a big family party. That's enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, and keep saving a little, about a hundred a month, because Raj's taxi money goes up and down. I'd ask Dev to teach me more about hen health over the winter. That's the part I want to get better at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the day after a big party when the house is clean again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the taxi money goes up and down. How do you manage that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My diner wages were steady, and the farm wages are steady, so we pay the bills with mine and save what we can from his. In a good month, Raj's money goes in the jar. In a bad month, we're careful. That's how my mother did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the usual. Egg prices, bird flu, whether the Mercers' son wants to take the farm over. Bird flu worries me more than any computer.

S0.say: I'd say that's a lot of worry over nothing, to the women in the packing room and at the community centre on Sunday. She'd leave posting online to her daughter.
S0.think: She'd be pleased: her job carries on until 66 and Raj keeps driving his taxi. She uses AI sometimes for hen problems and recipes, and that's enough.
S0.do: Keeps working at Ashgrove and saving about 100 a month as a buffer against Raj's uneven taxi income. Asks Dev the stockman to teach her more about hen health over the winter.
S0.feel: Calm, like the morning after a big party when the house is clean again.
S0.quote: Bird flu worries me more than any computer.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima's household finances are carefully managed in a way she learned from her mother. In a plateau, her real worries are farm risks like bird flu and succession. She wants to get better at the animal side, not the machine side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to work with it, like we always have. Farms had to change before and they'll change again. I'd say people should learn and not expect the government to fix everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the packing room would go first. The grader already does half of what we used to do by hand. If a machine can spot a cracked egg better than my eyes, then there's two of us in that room who aren't needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd see what the bigger egg farms do first. If they put in the camera machines for cracks, I'd ask Mrs Mercer if I can move to the hen houses full time and learn the birds properly. And I'd start saving a bit more, a hundred and fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when the diner's lunch crowd started getting thinner, before the bypass. You notice, and you start thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the diner's crowd getting thinner. What did you do then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not enough, honestly. I kept hoping. When it closed, I had three weeks' wages saved. I said to myself, never again. This time I'd watch and move earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the packing room would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena, who's been there twelve years. She's sixty-two and she's a widow. She's quicker than me at the packing, but she doesn't want to go near the sheds. I'd worry about her more than me.

S1.say: I'd say we have to work with it as we always have, and people should learn rather than expect the government to fix everything.
S1.think: She thinks the packing room goes first, since the grader already does half the work and a camera could spot cracks better than her eyes.
S1.do: Watches what bigger egg farms do, then asks Mrs Mercer to move her to the hen houses full time. Raises savings to about 150 a month.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like noticing the diner's lunch crowd thinning before the bypass.
S1.quote: When it closed, I had three weeks' wages saved. I said to myself, never again.
S1.fieldNote: The diner closure is Fatima's reference point, and she draws a clear lesson: move earlier this time. Her steadiness shows in waiting for bigger farms to go first. Her concern for her colleague Lena is genuine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, but it's no use crying. Families and communities will have to pull together. I'd say that at the community centre and to my children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be frightened for us. If the packing room goes, and Raj's taxi goes because the cars drive themselves, we both lose our work within two years. We'd have maybe four months of savings. My pension isn't until sixty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut back straight away, no more takeaways, and Raj would sell the second taxi plate he rents out. I'd start cooking for people, like I did at the diner, parties and weddings, from home. And I'd ask my children, Sana, Arjun and Kabir, if they could help us for a year or two, because that's what family is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I wouldn't sit and cry about it. I'd cook. That's how I deal with things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said family is for helping. Would you be comfortable asking your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfortable, no. Proud, a little bit hurt. But I raised them, I fed them, I paid for Sana's pharmacy school with diner shifts. If they help us for a year, that's not a handout. That's family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what would you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Raj we're doing the sums, and I'd ring every cousin who's ever had a wedding and say, I'm cooking now, tell your friends. When the bypass opened, nobody asked the diner. When the robots come, nobody will ask the hens. You just make your plans and feed your family.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast but there's no use crying, and families and communities will have to pull together.
S2.think: She'd be frightened: her packing job and Raj's taxi work could both go within two years, with about four months of savings and her pension not until 66.
S2.do: Cuts takeaways and Raj sells his rented-out second taxi plate straight away. Starts cooking from home for parties and weddings, calling every cousin in the first month, and asks her three children to help for a year or two.
S2.feel: Anxious but not crying about it; she'd cook, because that's how she copes.
S2.quote: If they help us for a year, that's not a handout. That's family.
S2.fieldNote: Fatima's traditional values come through in how she frames family help: earned, not a handout. Her instinct is to start working on something, specifically catering, rather than wait. The double risk to her and Raj is the core of her fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to get ready, so people should get ready, not complain. I'd say it to the young people at the community centre especially.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to sixty-three, and Raj to sixty-six, which is his pension. So it's not so bad. If I can keep working at Ashgrove a few more years and build up the cooking, we'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the cooking now, slowly, one event a month, and see if it grows. I'd do the food hygiene certificate properly, and I'd use the AI to help with the costing and menus, because Sana says it's good for that. And we'd keep saving a hundred and fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful. Five years is a proper amount of time to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They mean I can build the cooking before I need it, not after. In the fast picture I'd be ringing cousins in a panic. With five years, by the time the packing room changes, I'd already have regular customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want help from the government in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not really. Maybe fewer rules for small food businesses at home, because the forms are a nightmare. But I'd rather have customers than cheques.

S3.say: I'd say we've got time to get ready, so people should get ready and not complain, especially the young people at the community centre.
S3.think: Five years gets her to 63 and Raj to his pension at 66, so if she keeps working at Ashgrove and builds up the cooking, they'd be all right.
S3.do: Starts home catering slowly, one event a month, and takes the food hygiene certificate. Uses AI for costing and menus and keeps saving about 150 a month.
S3.feel: Uneasy but more hopeful, with time to build something.
S3.quote: But I'd rather have customers than cheques.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time lets Fatima build her catering business before she needs it. She would now use AI for costing, a step she'd take once her daughter vouched for it. Her one ask of government is fewer rules, not support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's plenty of time, and people should use it wisely. Learn something, save, help your family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. I'd be sixty-eight, retired, and Raj too. We'd have our pensions and maybe I'd still cook for weddings, because I'd want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Ashgrove until I stop at sixty-six. I'd keep saving, and I'd talk to Kabir, our youngest, about his work, because he's a bank clerk and that's the sort of job I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a long time away, and we'd have time to get everything in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kabir?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him what I learned from the diner: don't wait for the road to move. Learn a trade that needs your hands, or your face, something people still want from a person. He'd roll his eyes, but he'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you miss Ashgrove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. The hens, the packing room gossip, Mrs Mercer bringing in cake on a Friday. If robots do it in ten years, I'd hope someone still brings cake.

S4.say: I'd say that's plenty of time and people should use it wisely: learn something, save and help your family.
S4.think: For her it's fine: she and Raj would be retired at 68 with pensions, and she might still cook for weddings because she'd want to.
S4.do: Carries on at Ashgrove until stopping at 66 and keeps saving. Talks to her youngest son Kabir, a bank clerk, about changing his work.
S4.feel: Calm, with time to get everything in order.
S4.quote: Don't wait for the road to move.
S4.fieldNote: In the long picture Fatima's attention goes to her youngest son and his bank job. The diner lesson, don't wait for the road to move, is her core belief about change. Her fondness for the small social parts of farm life came through.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Both of us out of work, before our pensions, with only a few months saved. What would help is my children close by and a little catering business of my own. And fewer rules and costs for people starting a food business from their kitchen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about food. Everyone talks about robots making things, but people still want to sit and eat together. As long as that's true, someone who can cook will find work.

headlineQuote: When the bypass opened, nobody asked the diner. When the robots come, nobody will ask the hens. You just make your plans and feed your family.
portrait: Fatima Gupta is 58 and has worked for three years at Ashgrove, a farm with 12,000 free-range laying hens, potatoes and some beef, mostly in the egg-packing room and the hen houses. Before that she cooked for 25 years at a roadside diner that closed when the bypass opened. She takes up new tools once others have tried them, uses AI now and then for hen records and recipes, and believes in hard work, family and community rather than government help. She is calm about a plateau, uneasy with steady change because the packing room is already half machines, and anxious with AGI in two years because both her job and her husband Raj's taxi work would be at risk. With more warning she plans a small home catering business and leans on her three grown children, ending calm in the ten-year picture.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her packing job and Raj's taxi work could both go within two years, before either of them reaches pension age.
whatWouldHelp: Her children nearby and a small catering business of her own, plus fewer rules and costs for people starting small food businesses from home.
